533.title: The chariot leaves Ayodhya
533.hook: a king runs after a chariot, and his son keeps going: why Hindus call Rama maryada purushottama
533.howItsDone: In the text, the departure from Ayodhya moves slowly, and its lasting image is the old king watching the road until even the dust of the wheels is gone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the goodbyes: bark clothes, and Sumitra's verse, Ayodhya is wherever Rama is. Today, the chariot moves.

Look back, and you can't leave. Don't look back, and it feels cruel. That's the trouble with driving away from someone standing in a doorway, and it's Rama's trouble now. The charioteer Sumantra has the horses ready. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana climb in, with their weapons, a spade, a basket, and Sita's clothes for fourteen years. As the chariot starts to roll, the whole city starts to run after it.
screen: `LOOK BACK, OR GO ON?` → `THE CHARIOT STARTS TO ROLL.` → `THE CITY RUNS AFTER IT.`

segments.voice: Valmiki fills the streets with noise. People run beside the wheels, calling to Sumantra to slow down so they can see Rama's face a little longer. From the palace comes the old king himself, on foot, with Kausalya, crying: wait, Sumantra, wait. Rama hears his father. He can't bear it, and he can't stop. Go on, he tells the driver quietly. If the king asks later, say you didn't hear. Being told to stop and told to go is pain either way; better to make it short. The chariot pulls away, and Dasharatha watches until even the dust from the wheels is gone. But the people keep following, all the way to the Tamasa river, and the whole crowd sleeps on the bank around them. Rama lies awake. These people will follow us into the forest, he thinks, and lose their homes. So before dawn he and Sumantra harness the horses quietly, cross the river, and turn the chariot back and forth so the tracks can't be followed. Here's why Hindus treasure this scene. Rama's father is begging him to stop, and he doesn't, because stopping would break the word his father gave. Hindus call Rama maryada purushottama, the best of men, who keeps the bounds. Maryada is the line dharma draws, and Rama keeps it even when love is pulling the other way. But look how he keeps it: a goodbye made short, and a whole city spared. In the Ramayana, dharma is firm and kind at once. It's why Hindu families still hold Rama up as the one who keeps his word: hold the line you've promised, and spare the people you love what pain you can.

segments.voice: Many Hindus say Rama's name when the road is hard: just Ram, softly. If you pray, let it ride your out-breath for a few minutes, Ram, and rest in the in-breath between. If you don't pray, think of a goodbye you had to make; breathe in the pull to look back, breathe out the line you kept.

534.title: Guha, Rama's friend
534.hook: at the edge of the kingdom, on the bank of the Ganga, a forest king runs to meet his friend
534.carry: sakhya: loving God as a friend
534.tomorrow: The night watch on the Ganga
534.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor Guha as a model of devoted friendship; Shringaverapura, near Prayagraj, is visited by pilgrims as the place where Rama met him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the departure, and maryada. Rama kept his father's word while his father wept, and slipped away from the sleeping crowd at the Tamasa. Today, the Ganga, and a friend.

The chariot crosses river after river, through villages already talking about the prince who's been sent away. At the southern edge of the kingdom of Kosala, Rama turns in the chariot, faces the way they've come, and says goodbye to Ayodhya and its gods. Then they ride on to the Ganga. Near a town called Shringaverapura the river is wide and bright. And on its bank lives someone who has heard Rama is coming.
screen: `RIVER AFTER RIVER.` → `GOODBYE TO AYODHYA.` → `SOMEONE WAITS ON THE GANGA.`

segments.voice: His name is Guha, king of the Nishadas, a people who live by the forest and the river, hunting, fishing and running boats. Valmiki introduces him with one phrase: Rama's friend, as dear to him as his own life. Guha comes out with his family, carrying food and drink of every kind. Rama sees him from a distance, and before Guha can bow, Rama embraces him. Then Guha makes an extraordinary offer. This land is yours, as Ayodhya is. Stay. Rule here. Rama thanks him warmly and says no. He has vowed to live fourteen years as a forest ascetic, and he won't break it on his first day. He accepts one thing, and it's not for himself: please feed the horses; they're my father's, and he loves them. That night Guha and Lakshmana sit up by the fire, bows in hand, while Rama and Sita sleep on the ground. Hindus have a name for Guha's kind of love. The Bhagavata Purana lists nine forms of bhakti, nine ways of loving God, and one of them is sakhya: friendship. You can love God as a servant loves a master, or a child a parent; you can also love God as a friend, with no fear and no ceremony, just food carried down to the river. Devotional retellings treasure this scene for a second reason: Guha is a forest king, outside the royal world, and Rama's embrace doesn't ask who his family was. It just says friend.

If you don't, picture a friend who showed up for you when things were bad, and breathe out thanks.

535.title: The night watch on the Ganga
535.hook: two men keep watch by a fire all night, and at dawn two princes twist their hair into a vow
535.carry: jata: a vow you can see
535.howItsDone: Matted hair, jata, is worn by some Hindu ascetics as a sign of renunciation; many devotees offer their hair at temples such as Tirumala (Tirupati) to fulfill a vow.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Guha, king of the Nishadas, and sakhya, loving God as a friend. Today, the night watch on the riverbank.

The fire is low. Rama and Sita sleep on a bed of grass under a tree, a few feet away. Lakshmana sits up with his bow across his knees, wide awake. Guha comes and sits beside him. Late at night, beside someone outside the family, with the people you love asleep nearby, things get said that daylight keeps in. That's what happens on this riverbank before the night is out.
screen: `A LOW FIRE, A BOW ACROSS THE KNEES.` → `GUHA SITS DOWN BESIDE HIM.`

segments.voice: Guha speaks first, kindly. I've made a bed for you. Go and sleep. My people and I will keep watch; we know this forest. Lakshmana says no. How can I sleep, when my brother, who should be lying in a palace, is lying on the ground? Then he says out loud what he's carried all day: the old king, who he thinks won't survive the grief; the mothers, alone in the palace; the city, emptied of joy. Guha listens, and Valmiki says Guha weeps too. Two men, one grief. In the morning, Rama sends Sumantra home with the empty chariot, to comfort the king. Then he asks Guha for the milky sap of a banyan tree, and with it he and Lakshmana mat their hair into jata, the coils forest ascetics wear. Here's the teaching in that sap. Matted hair isn't a costume. It's a vow you can see. Forest ascetics stop caring for their hair as a sign they've left the palace behind, and Shiva himself is pictured with jata, the river Ganga caught in his locks. Hindus still mark a vow on the body. Many devotees offer their hair at the temple at Tirupati when a prayer is answered; some sadhus keep jata for life; and many families shave a child's first hair as an offering. When Rama twists banyan sap into his hair, he's saying with his whole head: I meant it. Now the only ones left are Rama, Sita, Lakshmana, and a friend with a boat.

536.title: Sita's prayer to the Ganga
536.hook: a boat on the Ganga, Sita's prayer in midstream, and a famous boatman who isn't in Valmiki
536.carry: the Ganga is Ganga Ma, a mother
536.howItsDone: Hindu pilgrims bathe in the Ganga, offer lamps and flowers to it, and speak to it as Ganga Ma, a mother goddess; many families keep Ganga water at home for puja and blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jata, a vow you can see, twisted into the princes' hair at dawn, after a night when two men shared one grief. Today, across the river.

If you've heard this part of the story at a temple or a family reading, you may remember a boatman who won't let Rama into his boat until he's washed his feet. He's afraid, he says with a grin, that the dust of those feet will turn his wooden boat into a woman, the way it once turned a stone into Ahalya. It's a lovely, funny scene. It comes from a later retelling, Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas. Valmiki's crossing is simpler, with its own quiet center.
screen: `WASH YOUR FEET FIRST.` → `A STORY FROM TULSIDAS.` → `VALMIKI'S CROSSING IS SIMPLER.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki, Guha arranges everything. He has a strong boat brought down to the bank, with oarsmen ready. Rama thanks him and says goodbye. Sita steps in first, then Lakshmana, then Rama, and the oarsmen push off into the current. In midstream, Sita folds her hands and speaks to the river itself, to Ganga, as a goddess. She asks Ganga to protect Rama through the fourteen years and bring the three of them back safely, and she vows to worship the river with offerings when they return. The first time the exiles leave dry land, Sita turns the crossing into worship. This is the teaching, and it's still alive. For Hindus, the Ganga is a goddess and a mother as well as a river: Ganga Ma, someone you can speak to. Pilgrims bathe in her and float lamps on her at dusk. Many families keep a small sealed pot of Ganga water at home, to sprinkle at a puja, bless a new house, or give a few drops to someone who is dying. The boat reaches the far bank. Rama sets an order for walking: Lakshmana first, Sita in the middle, Rama last, guarding them both. Guha watches from the shore until they're gone among the trees. So Valmiki's boatman isn't the comic figure of the later story. He's a king and a friend, and the one who stays on the bank, watching.

537.title: Bharadvaja's welcome
537.hook: smoke above the trees, a sage at the meeting of two rivers, and the oldest Hindu rule for guests
537.carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is God
537.howItsDone: Prayaga, now Prayagraj, is a place of pilgrimage; pilgrims bathe at the Sangam, where the Ganga and Yamuna meet, and the Kumbh Mela is held there.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganga Ma. Sita prayed to the river in midstream, and Guha watched them go. Today, a sage where two rivers meet.

segments.voice: Their first night alone, on the far side of the Ganga, is hard. Valmiki lets Rama's calm slip. He lies awake and worries out loud to Lakshmana: about his father, his mother, what Kaikeyi might do now. He even tells Lakshmana to go back and look after them. Lakshmana refuses. In the morning they walk on, and toward evening they see what a traveler in the forest hopes to see: smoke rising above the trees.
screen: `THE FIRST NIGHT ALONE.` → `RAMA WORRIES OUT LOUD.` → `SMOKE ABOVE THE TREES.`

segments.voice: Rama knows what the smoke means. That's the smoke of a sacred fire, he tells Lakshmana. A sage must live there. We must be near Prayaga, where the Ganga and the Yamuna meet. They follow the smoke to the hermitage of Bharadvaja, a great sage sitting by his fire among his students. Rama explains who they are, and Bharadvaja already knows. I heard you'd been sent away for no fault of your own. And then he welcomes them the old way: water for their feet, water for their hands, a seat, a cow, and food of the forest, fruit and roots. Look closely, because Hindus still do this. The Taittiriya Upanishad says it in three words: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be God to you. It's why a Hindu grandmother won't let anyone leave unfed. And it runs the other way too. When Hindus do puja, they welcome God like an honored guest, with the same gestures: water for the feet, water for the hands, a seat, food. The guest is treated like God, and God like a guest. Then Bharadvaja offers more: stay here for the fourteen years, at the holy meeting of the rivers. Rama declines. It's too close to home; people from the cities would keep coming to see us. Find us somewhere more secluded. Bharadvaja understands at once, and says he knows just the place.
screen: `THE SMOKE OF A SACRED FIRE.` · `PRAYAGA: WHERE TWO RIVERS MEET.` · `WATER FOR THE FEET, A SEAT, FOOD.` · `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA.` · then, large: `THE GUEST IS GOD.`

538.title: The road to Chitrakuta
538.hook: a sage gives directions the old way, and every river on the road becomes a prayer
538.carry: a tirtha is a holy crossing
538.howItsDone: In the text, Sita honors the Yamuna as she honored the Ganga; Hindus still go on tirtha yatra to holy rivers, and on Vat Savitri many women worship the banyan for their husbands' long lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday: atithi devo bhava. Bharadvaja welcomed the exiles as if they were God. Today, his directions.

Before maps on phones, directions were stories. Go past the old mill, turn at the big oak, and when you see the water tower, you're nearly there. Bharadvaja gives Rama directions like that the next morning: a river to cross, a tree to look for, a grove to walk through, and then a mountain. He's sending them to the place where they'll make their first home in exile, and he describes it with love.
screen: `DIRECTIONS WERE STORIES.` → `A RIVER, A TREE, A GROVE.` → `THEN A MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: There's a mountain, Bharadvaja says, about ten kroshas from here, called Chitrakuta. Sages live there. Peacocks call on its slopes, monkeys play in the trees, and there's fruit and honey everywhere. Then the route. Follow the Yamuna until you find a crossing. Build a raft, and cross. On the other side you'll find a great banyan with dark leaves, called Shyama, the dark one. People pray there. Walk on past it to a grove, and the road to the mountain. At the river, Rama and Lakshmana tie bamboo and dry wood together with creepers, and Lakshmana builds Sita a little seat of branches. In the middle of the Yamuna, as on the Ganga, Sita folds her hands and speaks to the river, asking for her husband's safe return and vowing offerings when they come home. On the far bank she bows to the dark banyan and prays again, for Rama, for Lakshmana, for the day they'll see their mothers. Every crossing gets a prayer. Hindus have a word for that: tirtha. It first meant a ford, a place to cross a river, and it came to mean a holy place, where, as many teachers put it, you cross over from the ordinary toward God. Prayaga, where they started, is one of the greatest tirthas, and a pilgrimage is a tirtha yatra, a journey of holy crossings. Sita's prayer at the tree has a living echo too: on the day called Vat Savitri, many Hindu women worship the banyan for their husbands' long lives.
screen: `A MOUNTAIN CALLED CHITRAKUTA.` · `A RAFT ACROSS THE YAMUNA.` · `A PRAYER AT THE DARK BANYAN.` · `TIRTHA: A FORD, A HOLY PLACE.` · then, large: `A JOURNEY OF HOLY CROSSINGS.`

539.title: A house of leaves
539.hook: the exiles reach the mountain, meet the poet telling their story, and bless a hut of leaves before stepping in
539.carry: griha pravesha: bless the home, then enter
539.howItsDone: Many Hindu families hold a griha pravesha, a house-entering ceremony, before moving into a new home; in the text, Rama blesses the leaf hut at Chitrakuta before the three exiles enter it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bharadvaja's directions, and tirthas, holy crossings. A raft across the Yamuna, a prayer at the dark banyan, and a mountain ahead. Today they arrive.

The forest is in flower. Rama walks with Sita, and for the first time since Ayodhya, he sounds almost happy. Look, he tells her: the flame-of-the-forest trees are in bloom, so red they look on fire. Honeycombs hang from the branches, big as buckets. Listen to the birds. Then the trees open, and there it is: a mountain with many peaks, streams running down its sides. Chitrakuta.
screen: `THE FOREST IN FLOWER.` → `TREES THAT LOOK ON FIRE.` → `THERE IT IS: CHITRAKUTA.`

segments.voice: Chitrakuta, or Chitrakoot as many say it today, means something like the bright peak, or the many-colored peak. Rama decides at once: we'll live here. But first, a visit. On the mountain is the hermitage of a sage, and the three exiles bow to him. The sage is Valmiki. Enjoy that for a second: the poet telling this whole story appears inside it, welcoming the hero he's writing about. Then the work. Lakshmana gathers wood and leaves and builds a hut, a parnashala, a house of leaves, strong against wind and rain, with a door and a thatched roof. And before anyone steps inside, Rama performs a rite to bless the house, with offerings to the gods of the dwelling. Only then do the three of them go in. Hindus still do this. Before a family moves into a new home, there's often a griha pravesha, a house-entering: a puja or a havan, a lamp, a pot of water, in many families milk boiled over on the new stove, and only then does anyone sleep there. The idea is simple and deep. A house isn't just walls. It's a place where God is invited to live with you, and you invite God first. Look how far this week has come: from a chariot leaving a weeping city, across two great rivers, to a house of leaves on a bright mountain, blessed before anyone stepped in.
screen: `CHITRAKUTA: THE BRIGHT PEAK.` · `VALMIKI, INSIDE HIS OWN STORY.` · `A PARNASHALA, A HOUSE OF LEAVES.` · `GRIHA PRAVESHA: BLESS, THEN ENTER.` · then, large: `INVITE GOD IN FIRST.`

segments.voice: Picture one corner of the place you live, a chair, a window, a doorway, the way Rama and Sita saw their hut that first night: small, new and theirs. If you pray, do what many Hindus do in a new home: picture a lamp lit in that corner, and ask God to live there with you. If you don't, breathe in gratitude for a roof, and breathe out the same wish for someone who doesn't have one.
